This is the first post on this blog. The idea is simple: take one question at a time, look at the data, and try to reason about it like an economist, carefully, with the mechanism spelled out and the obvious objections answered. It is a gym for training my thinking, and writing is the best method.

To check that everything works, here is a chart made in R directly inside the post. It uses the `economics` dataset that comes with ggplot2 (US monthly data from FRED).

```{r}
#| label: fig-unemployment
#| fig-cap: "Unemployed people as a share of the US population, 1967–2015. Source: FRED, via the ggplot2 `economics` dataset."
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)

economics$unemp_rate <- economics$unemploy / economics$pop * 100

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemp_rate)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f4e5f", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed, % of population") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fbfaf7", colour = NA))
```

(Note: this is unemployed people over the *total* population, not the official unemployment rate, which divides by the labour force. Spotting that kind of difference is part of the point of this blog.)
